analysis.one_liner: Invests heavily in affordable housing and down-payment help, paid for by raising estate taxes on the largest inheritances.
analysis.headline: Warren's housing bill — new funding for affordable homes and higher estate taxes on the biggest fortunes — died in committee with no cosponsors and was never voted on.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would spend tens of billions of dollars a year building and repairing affordable rental housing, offer down-payment grants to first-time buyers in neighborhoods that were historically redlined, help borrowers who owe more than their homes are worth, and force banks to serve low-income communities more fully. It also strengthens the Fair Housing Act to cover sexual orientation, gender identity, marital status, and source of income. To pay for it, the bill lowers the estate tax exemption to $3.5 million per person, raises rates to as high as 65%, adds a 10% surtax on billion-dollar estates, and closes common trust loopholes used by the wealthiest families.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters struggling with high housing costs (through new affordable construction funding), first-time homebuyers in formerly redlined or segregated neighborhoods (down-payment grants of up to 3.5% of a home's value), underwater homeowners (refinancing and principal-reduction grants), Native American communities (increased housing block grants), small businesses in low-income areas (stronger bank lending obligations), and renters protected from discrimination based on source of income or sexual orientation. Construction workers on funded projects would be guaranteed prevailing wages under the Davis-Bacon Act.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $44.5 billion per year for the Housing Trust Fund and $2.5 billion per year for the Capital Magnet Fund from fiscal 2019 through 2028, to build and preserve affordable rental housing for very low-income families.

Creates a Middle Class Housing Emergency Fund ($4 billion in fiscal 2019) for competitive grants to state housing finance agencies to build rental units affordable to people earning below 120% of area median income, plus $2 billion per year for local grants to states and cities that cut zoning barriers to affordable housing.

Provides down-payment grants of up to 3.5% of a home's value to first-time buyers below 120% of area median income living in census tracts that were graded 'hazardous' on redlining maps or zoned for non-White residents under segregated zoning codes.

Creates a $2 billion formula grant program to help borrowers whose homes are worth less than they owe, through loan modifications, principal reduction, and programs to buy and rehabilitate foreclosed homes.

Expands the Community Reinvestment Act to cover nonbank mortgage lenders, requires community benefits plans with measurable lending goals, and adds public hearings and comment periods when banks seek mergers or expansions — and boosts penalties for banks that fail to meet the credit needs of lower-income communities.

Amends the Fair Housing Act to prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, gender identity, marital status, and source of income (including housing vouchers), and requires housing agencies to analyze and reduce barriers that keep voucher families out of higher-opportunity neighborhoods.
Construction workers on projects funded by the new grants must be paid prevailing wages under the Davis-Bacon Act.

analysis.who_pays: The estates of the wealthiest households: the bill cuts the estate tax exemption to $3.5 million per person and raises rates to 55%–65% on estates above those levels, adds a 10% surtax on billion-dollar estates, requires grantor retained annuity trusts to run at least 10 years, applies transfer taxes to assets held in grantor trusts at death, eliminates the generation-skipping tax exemption for trusts lasting more than 50 years, and tightens annual gift-tax exclusions for hard-to-value transfers. Banks and nonbank mortgage lenders would face expanded examination, data-collection, and community-benefit obligations.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes very large new spending — $44.5 billion per year for the Housing Trust Fund alone, plus $2 billion per year in local grants, a $4 billion emergency fund, and other programs — all funded by shifting taxes onto large estates; taxpayers who favor smaller government or different housing priorities would bear the broader fiscal consequences.

Critics of estate tax increases commonly argue they burden family businesses and farms passed between generations; this bill sets the exemption at $3.5 million per individual ($7 million per couple), which shields most such estates but leaves very large ones facing rates up to 65% plus a 10% surtax above $1 billion.

The down-payment assistance targets buyers in formerly redlined, low-income areas; programs of this type can raise prices in exactly those neighborhoods if housing supply does not keep up, and the bill pairs the assistance with supply reforms that depend on local governments voluntarily adopting them.
Davis-Bacon prevailing-wage requirements raise construction costs on funded projects, which can reduce the number of units built per dollar.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the potential benefits are large: a serious national investment in affordable housing supply, direct down-payment help for families in historically excluded neighborhoods, and stronger protections against discrimination. The costs fall almost entirely on a narrow group — estates above $3.5 million per person and, above $1 billion, at rates up to 65% plus a 10% surtax — plus compliance costs for banks. The main honest reservations are the bill's scale of new appropriations, the possibility that demand-side help in tight markets raises prices before supply reforms take hold, and that it was never debated or amended, so its design was never tested. As written, the benefit-to-cost balance clearly favors working and middle-income households.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in September 2018, the committee never took it up, and the 115th Congress ended in January 2019, killing the bill.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on September 26, 2018.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action was ever taken — no committee hearing or markup, no committee report, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The wealthiest estates kept the larger exemption and lower rates set by the 2017 tax law, since the bill's higher estate taxes never advanced; banks and nonbank mortgage lenders avoided the expanded Community Reinvestment Act obligations; and restrictive local zoning could remain in place. Renters and first-time buyers in high-cost markets received none of the bill's promised housing investment.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee; it was never taken up.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation (Chaired by Sen. Orrin Hatch, R-UT, in 2018)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in September 2018 and never reported it, held no recorded markup or hearing on it, letting it die at the end of the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator joined as a cosponsor, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no measurable partisan or bipartisan support.

industries.industry: Ultra-wealthy households and the estate-planning industry
industries.note: The bill cuts the estate tax exemption to $3.5 million, raises top rates to 65%, adds a 10% surtax on billion-dollar estates, and closes GRAT, grantor-trust, and dynastic-trust loopholes that let the largest fortunes pass largely untaxed. Blocking the bill preserved the current low rates for these estates.

industries.industry: Banks, credit unions, and nonbank mortgage lenders
industries.note: The bill extends the Community Reinvestment Act to nonbank mortgage originators, requires community benefits plans and public hearings for mergers and expansions, mandates extensive new lending data collection, and increases penalties for failing to serve low-income communities. Those obligations are the mechanism for steering credit to ordinary borrowers.

Tens of billions per year in authorized funding for affordable construction, plus grants that reward cities for loosening zoning, would create sustained demand for multifamily and affordable housing construction, with prevailing-wage rules for workers.

Landlords could no longer reject tenants based on source of income (including vouchers), sexual orientation, gender identity, or marital status, and zoning reforms would add competing supply; owners of vacant land and existing units in low-supply markets would face downward pressure on rents.
